newsitem.title: GERMANY: Jobless surge causes alarm in Germany.
newsitem.headline: Jobless surge causes alarm in Germany.

text.p: A big surge in German unemployment ignited a heated debate on Friday over how to stop the jobs erosion while newspaper editorials criticised Helmut Kohl's government for lacking the vision to solve the problem.

With every German daily from the Baltic Sea to the Black Forest devoting much of their front pages to news that unemployment in January leaped by half a million to a post-war record 4.66 million, calls grew louder for fast and effective action.

"The unemployment numbers are catastrophic and it is clear the Kohl government is no longer able to solve our problems," said Gerhard Schroeder, state premier in Lower Saxony and a leader of the opposition Social Democrats (SPD).
"Kohl has become part of the problem," Schroeder told German television.
The Federal Labour Office said on Thursday the unemployment rate climbed to 12.2 percent in January from 10.8 percent in December, the highest in 64 years.
The chancellor is regularly ridiculed for forecasting unemployment will be halved by 2000, even as it rises further.

Kohl tried as usual to put an optimistic spin on the news, saying the unemployment rate would soon begin to fall. But he admitted the figures were the bleakest he has seen in his 14 years as chancellor.

Kohl's only comments on the massive leap in unemployment were made to his hometown newspaper, the Rheinpfalz in Ludwigshafen. He left Chancellery Minister Friedrich Bohl to fend off attacks on the government's policies.

"It is wrong to say we have misjudged the situation," Bohl told the ZDF television network. "The January figures are unacceptable. But the measures we introduced should mean that improvements can be expected in the second half of the year."

It was a predictable call for calm that newspaper editorials were ready to pounce all over. Conservative and liberal dailies filled their columns with dire warnings that major steps were needed to resolve the unemployment crisis.

They belittled the fact that government and opposition agree on only one idea -- cutting overtime hours -- to reduce unemployment, and blasted political leaders for failing to understand that old prescriptions will no longer work.

"Anyone who takes a sober look at unemployment should realise that it will be much harder to resolve than previously thought," Die Welt wrote. "The core of the problem is that labour in Germany is too inflexible and too expensive."

While warning comparisons to the high unemployment in the ill-fated Weimar Republic were out of place, the conservative Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung said lower taxes, deregulation, a smaller government and new thinking were needed.

"There are no longer any patent recipes," the FAZ said. "But what will definitely fail is the muddled attempt to push the social security system of yesterday into the business world of tomorrow. That will lead to a huge accident whose result will be mass unemployment."
The liberal Sueddeutsche Zeitung called Kohl's promise to halve unemployment a "4.66-million-man lie."
"Everyone is blaming everyone and everything else -- high labour costs, too much overtime, unpatriotic companies moving jobs abroad and the government with its misguided policies," the paper wrote.

"But no one can be bothered to take a hard look at what is really wrong," it added. "It should then become clear that the solutions of the old industrial age are no longer enough for the job market problems of the future."
